newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: C.Europe leaders summit to focus on EU integration.
newsitem.headline: C.Europe leaders summit to focus on EU integration.

text.p: Presidents of eight central European states, including Germany and Italy, are due to arrive in the Slovenian coastal resort of Piran on Friday to discuss European integration at their fourth annual meeting.

The presidents of Germany, Italy and Austria, all members of the European Union, will be joined by the heads of state of the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia -- former communist states which have made joining the EU and NATO their main foreign policy goals.
The Piran meeting is taking place 10 days ahead of a EU summit in Amsterdam where leaders are expected to sign a new treaty designed to prepare the 15-member bloc for enlargement into eastern Europe.
"A united, democratic and free Europe is the only good possibility that Europe and Slovenia have," Slovenian President Milan Kucan, who is hosting the meeting, told the Slovenian press agency STA.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are considered to be the most likely candidates to be included in a first round of EU expansion, with Slovenia figuring as an outside chance.
Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Romania have also applied to join the EU.

The informal two-day summit in Piran, the first large gathering of heads of state in the former Yugoslav republic, follows similar meetings in Poland last year, Hungary in 1995 and the Czech Republic in 1994.
Analysts said the meeting might prove helpful to Slovenia in its bid to join the EU as soon as possible. Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek has pinned his hopes of Slovenian EU entry by 2002.

"It is very positive that such a number of statesmen are meeting here as it will attract more attention to Slovenia ahead of the EU expansion decision," said Peter Stanovnik, head of the Institute for Economic Research at Ljubljana University.
While most of the presidents have few political decision-making powers, they are likely to use their influence to try to back the bids of their regional neighbours.

The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are almost certain to be invited to join NATO at its summit in Madrid in July but officials said the talks in Piran were not expected to focus on the expansion of the military alliance.
